explanation: Regular verbs in the present tense follow a predictable pattern. Remove the infinitive ending -en to get the stem, then add personal endings: -e (ich), -st (du), -t (er/sie/es), -en (wir), -t (ihr), -en (Sie/sie). Verbs whose stem ends in -t or -d insert an extra -e before -st and -t to make pronunciation easier.

exercises.explanation: First person singular: stem 'lern' + ending '-e' = lerne
Second person singular: stem 'spiel' + ending '-st' = spielst
First person plural always takes the full infinitive form for regular verbs: wohnen
Stem 'arbeit' ends in -t, so add '-et' for third person singular: arbeitet
Second person plural: stem 'trink' + ending '-t' = trinkt

explanation: The verbs sein (to be) and haben (to have) are the two most important irregular verbs in German. Their forms do not follow the regular pattern and must be memorised. Both are used very frequently — as main verbs and as auxiliary verbs in compound tenses.

exercises.explanation: First person singular of 'sein' is 'bin' — an irregular form.
Third person singular of 'haben' is 'hat'.
'haben' in first person plural keeps the full infinitive form.
Second person singular of 'sein' is 'bist'.

explanation: German main clauses follow a Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) order in their basic form. The verb is always the second element in a statement — this is called the 'V2 rule'. If you begin a sentence with something other than the subject (e.g. a time expression), the subject moves to third position, right after the verb.
examples: Am Wochenende besuchen wir meine Eltern.

exercises.explanation: Subject first, verb second, object and time expression follow.
Time expression first, then verb (V2), then subject.

exercises.prompt: Which word order is correct? (a) Heute ich gehe zum Arzt. (b) Heute gehe ich zum Arzt.
exercises.explanation: When 'heute' opens the sentence, the verb 'gehe' must remain second — so the subject 'ich' shifts to third position.
Subject 'Sie', verb 'liest', object 'das Buch'.

explanation: W-questions (Wh-questions) begin with a question word and ask for specific information. The question word comes first, followed immediately by the conjugated verb, then the subject. Common A1 question words: Wer (who), Was (what), Wo (where), Woher (where from), Wohin (where to), Wann (when), Wie (how), Wie viel (how much).

exercises.explanation: 'Was' asks about things or prices — 'What does that cost?'
'Woher' asks about origin — always use this, never 'Von wo' at A1 level.

exercises.prompt: Which question asks 'What is your name?'
exercises.explanation: 'Wie heißen Sie?' literally asks 'How are you called?' — the standard way to ask someone's name.
'Wann' asks about time.

explanation: Yes/no questions are formed by placing the conjugated verb first, before the subject. No question word is used. The answer is ja (yes) or nein (no). You can also use doch to contradict a negative question — this has no direct English equivalent.

exercises.explanation: Yes/no question: verb first, then subject.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: 'Bist du nicht müde?' You ARE tired. What do you answer?
exercises.explanation: 'Doch' contradicts a negative question — use it when the answer to a negative question is yes.
Yes/no questions begin with the conjugated verb.
Verb 'Ist' first, then demonstrative 'das', then subject 'Ihr Fahrrad'.

explanation: German nouns have three genders: masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das). The definite article (the) changes by gender: der, die, das. The indefinite article (a/an) is: ein (masculine/neuter), eine (feminine). In the accusative case — used when the noun is the direct object — only the masculine article changes: den / einen.
examples: Die Frau kauft eine Tasche. (Nominative/Accusative, feminine)
Das Kind spielt im Park. (Nominative, neuter)

exercises.explanation: Masculine noun in accusative: 'ein' becomes 'einen'.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct? (a) Das Buch ist interessant. (b) Der Buch ist interessant.
exercises.explanation: 'Buch' is neuter — use 'das'.
Neuter nominative definite article is 'das'.
Feminine indefinite article stays 'eine' in accusative.

exercises.prompt: Ich trinke ___ Kaffee. (der Kaffee, Akkusativ — unbestimmter Artikel gefragt)
exercises.explanation: Masculine noun in accusative takes 'einen'.

explanation: There are two ways to negate in German. Use 'kein/keine/kein' to negate a noun that has no article or an indefinite article — it follows the same endings as 'ein'. Use 'nicht' to negate verbs, adjectives, adverbs, or nouns with a definite article. 'Nicht' generally comes near the end of the clause.
examples: Ich habe kein Auto. (negating a noun with no article)
Ich komme nicht aus Deutschland. (negating a verb/adverb phrase)

exercises.prompt: Ich habe ___ Telefon. (I have no phone.)
exercises.explanation: 'Telefon' is neuter with no article — use 'kein' (neuter form).

exercises.prompt: Sie hat ___ Hunger. (She is not hungry.)
exercises.explanation: 'Hunger' is masculine and the direct object (accusative) — 'kein' takes accusative masculine ending: 'keinen'.

exercises.prompt: To negate 'Ich spreche Deutsch', which is correct? (a) Ich spreche kein Deutsch. (b) Ich spreche nicht Deutsch.
exercises.explanation: 'Deutsch' here is an unmodified noun used without an article — negate with 'kein'.
Negating an adjective: use 'nicht', placed before the adjective.

explanation:
Modal verbs modify the meaning of another verb. At A1, all six modals are in scope: können (can / to be able to), müssen (must / to have to), wollen (to want to), dürfen (to be allowed to), sollen (to be supposed to), möchten (would like to). The modal verb is conjugated in second position and the main verb goes to the end as an infinitive.

Conjugation overview (ich / du / er-sie-es / wir / ihr / sie-Sie):
• können: kann / kannst / kann / können / könnt / können
• müssen: muss / musst / muss / müssen / müsst / müssen
• wollen: will / willst / will / wollen / wollt / wollen
• dürfen: darf / darfst / darf / dürfen / dürft / dürfen
• sollen: soll / sollst / soll / sollen / sollt / sollen
• möchten: möchte / möchtest / möchte / möchten / möchtet / möchten

Note: ich and er/sie/es always have the same form for modals.
examples: Du musst um acht Uhr kommen.

exercises.explanation: First person singular of 'können' is 'kann' — irregular stem.
Second person singular of 'möchten' is 'möchtest'.

exercises.prompt: Where does the infinitive go in a modal verb sentence?
exercises.correctAnswer: At the end of the clause
exercises.explanation: In German, when a modal verb is used, the main verb (infinitive) is sent to the end of the sentence.
Modal 'möchte' is second, infinitive 'kaufen' goes to the end.
First person plural of 'können' returns to the infinitive form: 'können'.
Second person singular of 'müssen' is 'musst'.
Third person singular of 'wollen' is 'will' — irregular stem.
Third person singular of 'dürfen' is 'darf'.

exercises.prompt: Which modal means 'to be supposed to'? (a) wollen  (b) sollen  (c) dürfen
exercises.explanation: 'sollen' means you are supposed to do something — often because someone else has asked or instructed.

explanation: Separable verbs are made up of a base verb and a prefix (e.g. an-, auf-, ein-, mit-, zurück-). In a main clause, the prefix separates from the verb and moves to the very end of the sentence, while the conjugated base verb stays in second position. Common A1 separable verbs: anrufen (to call), aufstehen (to get up), einkaufen (to shop), anfangen (to begin), mitnehmen (to take along).
examples: Der Kurs fängt um neun Uhr an.
Nehmen Sie bitte Ihren Ausweis mit.
Sie steht um sechs Uhr auf.

exercises.explanation: Conjugated base 'stehe' stays in position 2; prefix 'auf' moves to the end.
'anrufen' → base 'ruft' + prefix 'an' at the end.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses 'einkaufen'? (a) Ich einkaufe heute. (b) Ich kaufe heute ein.
exercises.explanation: The prefix 'ein' must detach and move to the end of the clause.
Time word first, conjugated 'kaufen' second (V2 rule), subject 'wir' third, prefix 'ein' at the end.

explanation:
Possessive articles show ownership. All eight are in scope at A1: mein (my), dein (your, informal singular), sein (his), ihr (her), unser (our), euer (your, plural informal), ihr (their), Ihr (your, formal). They all take the same endings as the indefinite article 'ein'.

Ending overview: masculine nominative = no ending; feminine nominative/accusative = -e; neuter nominative/accusative = no ending; masculine accusative = -en.

Examples by possessive:
• mein / meine / mein / meinen
• dein / deine / dein / deinen
• sein / seine / sein / seinen  (his — use for male owners)
• ihr / ihre / ihr / ihren  (her — use for female owners)
• unser / unsere / unser / unseren
• euer / eure / euer / euren
• ihr / ihre / ihr / ihren  (their)
• Ihr / Ihre / Ihr / Ihren  (formal you)

Key rule: the possessive agrees with the grammatical gender and case of the THING owned, not the owner.
examples: Das ist mein Buch. (neuter nominative — no ending)
Ich habe meinen Bruder angerufen. (masculine accusative — -en)
Das ist sein Schlüssel. (his key — masculine nominative)
Wo ist ihre Jacke? (her jacket — feminine nominative)
Ist das Ihr Pass? (formal your — masculine nominative)

exercises.prompt: Das ist ___ (my) Schlüssel. (der Schlüssel — masculine nominative)
exercises.explanation: Masculine nominative: 'mein' — no ending.

exercises.prompt: Ich suche ___ (my) Tasche. (die Tasche — feminine accusative)
exercises.explanation: Feminine accusative: 'meine' — the -e ending stays the same as nominative.

exercises.prompt: Hast du ___ Handy? (your — informal, das Handy — neuter accusative)
exercises.explanation: Neuter accusative: 'dein' — no ending, same as nominative.

exercises.prompt: Ich besuche ___ (my) Vater. (der Vater — masculine accusative)
exercises.explanation: Masculine accusative: 'mein' + '-en' = 'meinen'.

exercises.prompt: Das ist Peter. Das ist ___ (his) Fahrrad. (das Fahrrad — neuter nominative)
exercises.explanation: Peter is male, so use 'sein' (his). Neuter nominative — no ending: 'sein'.

exercises.prompt: Das ist Maria. Ich kenne ___ (her) Bruder. (der Bruder — masculine accusative)
exercises.explanation: Maria is female, so use 'ihr' (her). Masculine accusative: 'ihr' + '-en' = 'ihren'.

exercises.prompt: Wir haben ___ (our) Haus verkauft. (das Haus — neuter accusative)
exercises.explanation: Neuter accusative: 'unser' — no ending.

exercises.prompt: A bank employee asks a customer: '___ Name, bitte?' (your, formal — der Name, nominative)
exercises.explanation: 'Ihr' (capital I) is the formal 'your'. Masculine nominative — no ending: 'Ihr Name'.

explanation:
The imperative (command form) exists in three forms at A1:

• Sie-Imperativ (formal): use the regular Sie-conjugation with the verb first. 'Kommen Sie bitte herein!' This is highest-frequency in formal contexts and exam exercises.

• du-Imperativ (informal singular): take the verb stem and drop the -st ending. Regular verbs: 'Lern!' / 'Komm!' / 'Hör zu!'. Verbs with e→i or e→ie vowel change in the present keep that change: sprechen → 'Sprich!', lesen → 'Lies!', essen → 'Iss!'. Verbs with a→ä do NOT change in the du-imperative: fahren → 'Fahr!' (not 'Fähr!').

• ihr-Imperativ (informal plural): use the ihr-conjugation without the word 'ihr'. 'Kommt bitte!' / 'Esst euer Brot!' / 'Lest den Text!'

All three forms can add 'bitte' to soften the command.
examples: Sprich bitte langsam! (du-form — e→i change: sprechen)
Lies das Buch! (du-form — e→ie change: lesen)

exercises.explanation: Sie-imperative: conjugated verb first, then 'Sie', then the rest of the sentence.
Sie-imperative of 'kommen' is 'Kommen' — the same as the Sie-conjugation.

exercises.prompt: How do you politely tell a customer to fill out a form?
exercises.correctAnswer: Füllen Sie das Formular aus, bitte.
exercises.explanation: Sie-imperative with separable verb: base verb first, prefix at the end.
Sie-imperative of 'warten': 'Warten Sie bitte!'

exercises.prompt: ___ (sprechen — du-Imperativ, e→i vowel change) bitte langsam!
exercises.explanation: du-Imperativ of 'sprechen': e changes to i in the du-form → 'sprich'. No ending added.

exercises.prompt: ___ (lesen — du-Imperativ, e→ie vowel change) den Text!
exercises.explanation: du-Imperativ of 'lesen': e→ie vowel change → 'lies'. No ending.

exercises.prompt: You are speaking to two friends. How do you say 'Come here, please!' (ihr-form of kommen)?
exercises.explanation: ihr-Imperativ = ihr-conjugation without 'ihr'. 'ihr kommt' → 'Kommt!' Add 'bitte' to soften.

topic: Präpositionen mit Dativ — Ortsangaben und Temporalangaben [PEDAGOGY-REWRITE]
explanation:
Several prepositions always take the dative case in German.

A) Location prepositions (Wo? — static place): in, an, auf, neben, zwischen, unter, über, vor, hinter. Dative changes the article: der/das → dem, die → der. Contractions: in + dem = im, an + dem = am.

B) Pure dative prepositions for movement and connection (highest frequency): mit (with / by means of), von (from), zu (to), bei (at / near), aus (from / out of), nach (to — for cities and countries). Common contractions: zu + dem = zum, zu + der = zur, von + dem = vom, bei + dem = beim.

C) Time prepositions (Wann? — temporal): am (days of the week and parts of the day: am Montag, am Morgen), im (months and seasons: im Januar, im Sommer), um (clock times: um drei Uhr), von...bis (a time range: von neun bis siebzehn Uhr).
examples: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. (location — der Tisch → dem Tisch)
Ich bin in der Schule. (location — die Schule → der Schule)
Das Café ist im Bahnhof. (in + dem = im)
Ich fahre mit dem Bus zur Arbeit. (mit + Dativ; zu + der = zur)
Am Montag gehe ich zum Arzt. (temporal am; zu + dem = zum)
Im Juli fahren wir nach Berlin. (temporal im + month)

exercises.prompt: Das Buch liegt auf ___ Tisch. (der Tisch → dative)
exercises.explanation: Masculine noun in dative: 'der' → 'dem'.

exercises.prompt: Ich bin in ___ Küche. (die Küche → dative)
exercises.explanation: Feminine noun in dative: 'die' → 'der'.

exercises.prompt: Which contraction is correct for 'in dem Supermarkt'?
exercises.explanation: 'in + dem' contracts to 'im' in spoken and written German.

exercises.prompt: Er wohnt ___ ___ Bahnhof. (near: neben + der Bahnhof)
exercises.explanation: 'neben' takes dative; 'der Bahnhof' is masculine → 'dem Bahnhof'.

exercises.prompt: Wir treffen uns ___ Marktplatz. (an + dem — contract it)
exercises.explanation: 'an + dem' contracts to 'am'. Always use this contraction in natural speech.

exercises.prompt: Ich fahre ___ dem Bus zur Schule.
exercises.explanation: 'mit' + dative = by means of. 'mit dem Bus' = by bus.
Use 'am' for days of the week: am Montag, am Dienstag, am Wochenende.

exercises.prompt: ___ August fahren wir in den Urlaub.
exercises.explanation: Use 'im' for months and seasons: im August, im Sommer, im Winter.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means 'from Monday to Friday'?
exercises.explanation: 'von...bis' expresses a time range. Both words are used together.

topic: Perfekt mit haben und sein — Partizip II [PEDAGOGY-REWRITE]
explanation:
The Perfekt (present perfect) is the main past tense used in spoken German and for A1 writing tasks such as a Wochenende-Bericht. It is formed with a helper verb (haben or sein) in position 2 and the Partizip II at the end of the sentence — this is called the Perfekt-Klammer.

Forming the Partizip II:
• Regular verbs: ge- + stem + -t → gemacht, gekauft, gelernt, gearbeitet, gespielt
• Irregular verbs: ge- + changed stem + -en → gegangen, gekommen, gefahren, gegessen, getrunken, geblieben

Choosing haben or sein:
• Use sein with verbs of movement from place to place (gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen) and with bleiben and sein itself.
• Use haben with all other verbs (this is the safe default): essen, trinken, kaufen, lernen, arbeiten, schlafen, lesen, schreiben, sprechen.

Perfekt word order: helper verb in position 2, Partizip II at the end.
• Ich habe gestern Pizza gegessen.
• Wir sind nach Berlin gefahren.

Präteritum war/hatte: at A1 only sein and haben use the Präteritum. war = was (all forms: ich war, du warst, er/sie/es war, wir waren, ihr wart, sie/Sie waren). hatte = had (ich hatte, du hattest, er/sie/es hatte, wir hatten, ihr hattet, sie/Sie hatten). Use these for past states: Ich war müde. Wir hatten Hunger.
examples: Ich habe gelernt. (regular: ge- + lern + -t; haben)
Sie hat gearbeitet. (regular: ge- + arbeit + -et; haben)
Sie ist geblieben. (irregular; sein — bleiben takes sein)
Ich habe Wasser getrunken. (irregular; haben — default)

exercises.prompt: Ich ___ gestern viel ___ (lernen — Partizip II bilden).
exercises.explanation: Regular verb: ge- + lern + -t = gelernt. Helper verb: haben (default).
Irregular Partizip II: gegessen. 'essen' takes haben — not a movement verb.

exercises.prompt: Er ___ um neun Uhr nach Hause ___. (gehen — Partizip II)
exercises.explanation: Irregular Partizip II: gegangen. 'gehen' takes sein — it expresses movement.

exercises.prompt: Which helper verb do you use with 'fahren' in the Perfekt?
exercises.explanation: 'fahren' expresses movement from A to B — it takes 'sein' as its helper verb.
Perfekt-Klammer: helper verb 'habe' in position 2, Partizip II 'getrunken' at the end.

exercises.prompt: Letzte Woche ___ ich in Berlin. (past state of sein)
exercises.explanation: Use 'war' (Präteritum of sein) for past states: Ich war in Berlin. = I was in Berlin.

exercises.prompt: Das Kind ___ gestern Fieber. (past state of haben)
exercises.explanation: Use 'hatte' (Präteritum of haben) for past states: Das Kind hatte Fieber. = The child had a fever.

explanation:
Some German verbs change their stem vowel in the du- and er/sie/es-forms of the present tense. The personal endings are the same as regular verbs — only the vowel in the stem changes.

Three patterns:
1. a → ä: fahren (du fährst, er fährt), schlafen (du schläfst, er schläft)
2. e → i: essen (du isst, er isst), geben (du gibst, er gibt), sprechen (du sprichst, er spricht), nehmen (du nimmst, er nimmt — also consonant doubling)
3. e → ie: lesen (du liest, er liest), sehen (du siehst, er sieht)

Only the du- and er/sie/es-forms are affected. All other forms (ich, wir, ihr, Sie/sie) use the normal stem.
examples: Du fährst mit dem Bus. (fahren: a→ä)
Er schläft bis neun Uhr. (schlafen: a→ä)
Er spricht Deutsch und Englisch. (sprechen: e→i)
Er gibt mir das Brot. (geben: e→i)
Du nimmst den Bus. (nehmen: e→i, plus consonant doubling)

exercises.explanation: 'fahren' has a→ä vowel change in er/sie/es: fährt.
'schlafen' has a→ä vowel change in du: schläfst.
'lesen' has e→ie vowel change in er/sie/es: liest.
'sprechen' has e→i vowel change in du: sprichst.

exercises.prompt: Which forms of a verb show the stem vowel change? (a) ich and wir  (b) du and er/sie/es  (c) ihr and Sie
exercises.explanation: Only the du- and er/sie/es-forms show the stem vowel change. All other persons use the regular stem.
'essen' has e→i vowel change in er/sie/es: isst.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'sehen' is correct for 'du'? (a) du seht  (b) du sehst  (c) du siehst
exercises.explanation: 'sehen' has e→ie vowel change in the du-form: du siehst.
